title: Life Admin · Episode 2
chapters: Buying big things without the debt trap
Making an insurance claim that sticks

units.t: Life Admin. Episode two.
In this episode: Buying big things without the debt trap, Private health insurance, decoded and Making an insurance claim that sticks.
Part one. Buying big things without the debt trap.
A new fridge, a laptop, a couch: big purchases often come with a tempting offer to pay later.
Here is how buy now pay later, interest-free deals and rent-to-own really work, and a better way to buy.
How pay-later works.
At checkout, a friendly line appears: four easy payments, no interest.
A thousand-dollar purchase suddenly looks like a few hundred.
That shift in feeling is the point.
Splitting a cost makes it easier to say yes, and research suggests people tend to spend more when paying feels less painful.
Buy now pay later typically means four payments over about six weeks, the first upfront.
Many charge no interest, earning money from retailers' fees and customers' late or account fees.
Since mid-2025, BNPL has been regulated as credit, so providers need a credit licence and must check the product isn't unsuitable for you.
The risks are several plans across providers, missed-payment fees and credit report problems.
This is general information, not financial advice.
Interest-free fine print.
Furniture and electronics stores often advertise long interest-free periods, perhaps a year or more, through a store card or finance partner.
These can be useful if you pay the full amount within the period.
The trap is what happens if you don't.
Any remaining balance usually starts attracting a high rate, often similar to a credit card.
Many of these products also charge a monthly account fee, and some an establishment fee, so the deal isn't truly free.
The account may stay open for future purchases.
Before signing, ask three questions: what is the rate after the interest-free period, what are the fees, and what is the minimum repayment?
Rent-to-own leases.
Some businesses offer appliances, furniture or electronics on a weekly lease, sometimes promoted to people on Centrelink payments with deductions taken straight from their payments.
These leases can cost much more than the retail price, and at the end you may not own the item.
ASIC has repeatedly warned about the high cost of some leases.
If you need an essential like a fridge or washing machine and can't afford it, look at alternatives first.
The No Interest Loan Scheme, run by Good Shepherd with community partners, offers loans for essential goods to eligible people on low incomes, with no interest or fees.
Services Australia may also offer an advance payment if you receive certain payments.
Pause and find the total.
A simple habit stops most regretful purchases: wait.
For anything over an amount you choose, perhaps a few hundred dollars, give yourself 48 hours, or a week for bigger items.
If you still want it, it's probably a considered decision rather than an impulse.
Next, work out the total cost, not the instalment.
Add up every payment and fee if you use credit.
Then ask a blunt question: if I had to pay the full price today from my own money, would I still buy it?
If not, the payment plan is making the decision for you.
Check that your existing repayments plus this one still leave room for rent, bills and food.
Save first, buy smarter.
The cheapest way to buy something big is usually to save first.
A sinking fund is money set aside regularly for a known future cost, such as a laptop, car registration or a replacement fridge.
Divide the expected price by the pay cycles until you need it, and automate a transfer into a separate account on payday.
You earn a little interest instead of paying it, and cash can give you bargaining power.
Ask politely whether paying upfront gets a better price.
Compare prices across retailers, and be wary of 'sale' prices that aren't real bargains.
Consider quality secondhand goods.
New goods come with automatic consumer guarantees under the Australian Consumer Law, which can matter more than an extended warranty.
The key idea: Pay-later offers make big prices feel small, and the risks come from stacking plans and missing payments.
Part two. Private health insurance, decoded.
Gold, Silver, Bronze, extras, excesses and a mysterious loading after 30.
Here is how private health insurance really works in Australia, so you can decide what you need.
Medicare, choice and tax.
Every Australian resident enrolled in Medicare can be treated free as a public patient in a public hospital.
So why do close to half of Australians hold private hospital cover?
Mostly for choice and timing.
As a private patient you can usually choose your specialist and hospital, and elective surgery such as a knee reconstruction may happen sooner than on a public waiting list.
Tax rules push some people towards cover as well.
The Medicare Levy Surcharge is an extra tax on people above an income threshold who lack appropriate hospital cover.
Separately, the Australian Government Rebate reduces premiums for many people, depending on income and age.
Check current figures at ato.
gov.
au.
Whether cover is worth it depends on your health, age, income and priorities.
This is general information, not financial advice.
Hospital tiers and extras.
Hospital cover pays towards your costs as a private patient, such as accommodation, theatre fees and part of the doctors' fees.
Since 2019, policies sit in four tiers: Gold, Silver, Bronze and Basic.
Each must cover a minimum list of clinical categories.
Gold covers all of them, including pregnancy and birth and joint replacements, while a cheap Basic policy may cover very little.
A 'plus' label means extra categories.
Compare the treatments you might realistically need, not just the tier name or price.
Extras pays part of the cost of services outside hospital, such as dental, physio and optical.
Each service has a benefit amount and an annual limit, so you pay the rest.
Add up what you actually spend, then compare it with the premium plus the gaps.
Excess, gaps, waiting periods.
Two policies in the same tier can cost very different amounts because of the excess, the amount you agree to pay upfront if you are admitted to hospital.
A higher excess lowers your premium but raises your bill when you need care.
You may also face a gap, the difference between what a doctor charges and what Medicare and your insurer pay.
Ask your specialist and hospital about likely gaps before treatment, and whether they have an arrangement with your fund.
Waiting periods apply when you first take out cover or upgrade.
They are commonly up to 12 months for pre-existing conditions and pregnancy, and shorter for most other hospital treatment.
Check the specifics before you need them.
Lifetime Health Cover loading.
Lifetime Health Cover encourages people to join earlier.

If you do not hold private hospital cover by 1 July following your 31st birthday, a loading of 2 per cent is added to your hospital premium for every year you are over 30 when you eventually join, up to a maximum of 70 per cent.
Someone first joining at 40 would typically pay around 20 per cent more than someone who joined at 30.
The loading is removed after you have held hospital cover continuously for 10 years.
Some exceptions exist, including for people who arrived in Australia later in life.
Extras-only cover does not count towards avoiding the loading.
Compare and switch.
Insurers have thousands of policies, and names alone tell you little.
The government website privatehealth.
gov.
au, managed by the Commonwealth Ombudsman, lets you compare policies from all registered funds, and every policy has a standard information statement summarising what it covers.
Commercial comparison sites can help, but they may not list every fund.
You can switch funds.
If you move to an equivalent level of hospital cover you generally will not serve the same waiting periods again, though upgrades may attract new ones.
Review your cover each year, especially when life changes, such as planning a family or retiring.
If you have a dispute with your fund, the Commonwealth Ombudsman can help, free of charge.
A tax agent can help you apply the tax rules to your situation.
The key idea: Private cover sits on top of Medicare, mainly for choice and timing, and tax rules also nudge people towards it.
Part three. Making an insurance claim that sticks.
You pay premiums for years hoping you never need them.
When something finally goes wrong, how you handle the first days of a claim can make a real difference to the outcome.
Prepare before disaster.
The best time to prepare for a claim is a quiet weekday, long before a storm or break-in.
Download your product disclosure statement, the long document that sets out what your policy covers, and read the sections on exclusions and how claims work.
Check your sum insured for home and contents.
Underinsurance is common, because people guess the value of their belongings and fall well short.
Many insurers offer online calculators for rebuilding or replacement costs.
Film each room and store the video in the cloud, along with receipts for expensive items.
Note your excess, the amount you pay towards each claim.
This is general information, not advice; read your own policy.
Make safe, then document.
Imagine coming home to water pouring through the ceiling.
Safety comes first: turn off water or power if it is safe, and call emergency services if anyone is in danger.
Policies generally expect reasonable steps to prevent further damage, such as a tarp or an emergency plumber, and those costs are often covered.
Before you throw anything away, photograph and film the damage, including serial numbers and brand labels.
Keep damaged items until the insurer says you may dispose of them.
After a car crash, exchange names, contact details, registrations and insurer details, photograph the scene, collect witness details and don't admit fault, as that is for insurers to work out.
Report theft to police and record the event number.
Lodge and keep a log.
Contact your insurer as soon as practical, through their app, website or claims line.
Delays can complicate a claim, especially if damage worsens.
You will receive a claim number; write it on every document and email.
Start a simple claim log on paper or in a notes app.
Record the date and time of every call, who you spoke to and what was agreed.
Follow up important calls with a short email confirming what was said.
Be honest and accurate in everything you tell the insurer.
Exaggerating a claim, even slightly, can give the insurer grounds to refuse it or cancel your policy, and it can have serious legal consequences.
Assessors and settlement.
For larger claims, the insurer may send an assessor or ask for quotes from builders.
You can generally supply your own quotes, and it is reasonable to ask for a copy of the assessor's report.
Insurers may offer to manage repairs through their own builders, or offer a cash settlement.
Cash can seem attractive, but check that it would cover the real cost of fixing the damage with a licensed tradesperson.
Once you accept it, the insurer usually has no further responsibility for the repairs.
Ask how the figure was calculated.
Keep receipts for temporary accommodation and emergency costs, as some policies cover these up to a limit.
Decisions and disputes.
Insurers that subscribe to the General Insurance Code of Practice commit to keeping you updated, deciding within set timeframes and explaining their reasons.
If your claim is denied, ask in writing for the decision, the policy wording relied on and any reports used.
Sometimes a refusal rests on a misunderstanding that extra evidence, like a receipt or tradesperson's report, can fix.
If you still disagree, make a formal written complaint, use the word 'complaint', and say what outcome you want.
Most complaints should get a response within about 30 calendar days.
If you are unhappy or hear nothing, lodge a complaint with the Australian Financial Complaints Authority at afca.
org.
au.
It is free for consumers and independent of insurers, and its decisions can bind the insurer.
The key idea: Know your policy, sum insured and excess before you need to claim, because underinsurance is common.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Since mid-2025, how is buy now pay later regulated in Australia?
Answer. As a form of credit requiring a licence.
Question two. What is a main reason Australians hold private hospital cover?
Answer. Choice of specialist and sooner elective surgery.
Question three. Why is it worth checking your sum insured before anything goes wrong?
Answer. Underinsurance is common and costly.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
